findings.paper_title: SBC Internal Audit Annual Conclusion 2025 -26
findings.headline: Council operating under government-appointed commissioners following 2024 Best Value failure
findings.detail: The document notes the council is operating with government-appointed commissioners following a 2024 Best Value review, which was the trigger for the Improvement and Recovery Plan. This is a regulatory intervention indicating serious governance or service delivery concerns.
findings.matters: Commissioner-led councils are at elevated risk. A lender must understand the causes of the Best Value failure and the credibility of the recovery plan.
findings.figures: 2024 Best Value review triggered appointment
findings.quote: The Council continue to operate with the governments appointed Commissioners following the 2024 Best Value review.

findings.paper_title: Audit Amendments Cover Report
findings.headline: Internal audit identified control weaknesses in credit note approval, debt monitoring, payment plans, and write-off records
findings.detail: A 2025 internal audit of sundry debt processes found inconsistencies in credit note approval, reminder letter timeframes, hold case monitoring, debt ownership, payment plans, invoice cancellation documentation, and write-off records. The council is responding with formal amendments to the Financial Regulations to strengthen controls and improve consistency across services.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses in income and debt management affect a council's financial resilience and audit assurance; a lender would want to understand that the council has identified the gaps and is remediating them systematically.
findings.figures: Approximately eight members of staff will require time to review and familiarise themselves with the amendments
findings.quote: Internal Audit findings showed some inconsistencies in credit note approval, reminder letter timeframes, hold case monitoring, debt ownership, payment plans, invoice cancellation documentation, and write-off- records.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: £26.3m investment property sinking funds being repurposed to close general budget gaps rather than their original purpose
findings.detail: The council holds £26.261m in Acquired Properties sinking funds earmarked to smooth rental income volatility. These are now being repurposed to cover general revenue budget gaps instead, showing the council is cannibalizing reserves set aside for specific purposes.
findings.matters: The asset disposal programme removes the investment income stream that these reserves were designed to protect. The council is now using these funds for day-to-day shortfalls, signalling revenue sustainability problems independent of the investment portfolio.
findings.figures: £26.261m in Acquired Properties Fund (73% of total earmarked reserves at 31.12.25)
findings.quote: Acquired Properties Fund Sinking Funds related to the management, maintenance, or development of the Council's investment properties... 26,261 [and] Instead, there is now a short to medium term period of additional Revenue Budget pressure, part of which could be eased by apply some use of re-purposed Sinking Funds reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: Earmarked revenue reserves depleting by 95% in four years as gap-closing mechanism
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves are projected to fall from £40.862m to £2.033m by 2028/29 as the council uses reserves to close budget gaps: £19.141m in 2025/26, £11.597m in 2026/27, £4.155m in 2027/28, and £3.936m in 2028/29. This approach exhausts the council's financial buffer entirely.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves to zero removes all flexibility to absorb unexpected events or changes. When reserves are gone, any further pressure requires either immediate cuts or new borrowing.
findings.quote: Opening Balance Earmarked Reserves 40,862 21,721 10,124 5,968 [continuing to closing balance 2,033]. In-year usage of available reserves to close budget gap (19,141) (11,597) (4,155) (3,936)

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: Projected budget gaps of £8.8m in 2026/27 and £3.6m in 2027/28 even after planned reserve usage
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy shows the council cannot balance its budget from revenue alone. Gaps of £8.8m in 2026/27, £3.6m in 2027/28, and £3.4m in 2028/29 persist even after planned drawdown of reserves, indicating structural deficit.
findings.matters: The council has no savings plan to close these gaps through efficiency or income; instead, it is consuming reserves. Once reserves are depleted, the council (or successor unitary) has no buffer.
findings.quote: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy is currently projected budget gaps for 2026/27 to 2028/29 as shown in the Table below. [Budget Gaps after in year use of reserves: 26-27 £m 8.8, 27-28 £m 3.6, 28-29 £m 3.4]

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: £7m unplanned MRP charge in 2025/26 from aborted capital projects
findings.detail: The council faces an unexpected £7m revenue charge in 2025/26 because capital projects have been abandoned and accounting rules require MRP to be applied on the resulting 'surplus assets'. This was not anticipated in the original budget and required use of reserves to offset.
findings.matters: Shows capital planning failures and unplanned pressures that consume reserves. It indicates projects previously expected to deliver did not proceed.
findings.figures: £7m additional MRP
findings.quote: In 2025/26 there is an additional £7m of MRP being applied to Revenue relating to MRP on surplus assets (in line with accounting requirements that once capital projects are aborted that MRP starts to be applied).

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - Reserves Strategy
findings.headline: Council subject to Best Value intervention directing investment asset disposal
findings.detail: Central government has imposed Best Value intervention, directing the council to undertake a comprehensive disposal programme of its investment property portfolio to reduce financial risk. This indicates prior governance or performance failures.
findings.matters: Best Value intervention is a serious governance marker and signals prior failures in financial or operational performance. It constrains the council's strategic options and is passed to the successor unitary authority.
findings.figures: £26.261m held in Acquired Properties sinking funds
findings.quote: The Best Value intervention has directed the Council to reduce this risk for itself and the successor unitary by undertaking a comprehensive investment assets disposal programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Unavoidable Expenditure Pressures 2026-27
findings.headline: Team capacity constraints forcing use of contractors for masterplan delivery
findings.detail: The council's Strategic Planning team lacks capacity to deliver the Integrated Improvement Plan masterplan work internally and is therefore procuring external contractors. The document notes that 'Officer time required to deliver the Masterplan is beyond the capacity of the Team' and cites the 'LGR environment' (Local Government Reorganisation) and 'recent challenges with recruitment to fixed term roles'.
findings.matters: Inability to recruit and retain staff to deliver statutory planning work signals institutional strain; contractors are a cost premium and a delivery risk if continuity is broken.
findings.figures: £82.5k consultancy + £60k contractor FTE for masterplan work (with further costs for external experts not yet quantified)
findings.quote: The Officer time required to deliver the Masterplan is beyond the capacity of the Team. Resource requirements (in time and experience) for the development of the Design Code indicate that delivery of the masterplan at pace will require 1x fte at a senior level.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Unavoidable Expenditure Pressures 2026-27
findings.headline: Supported housing operational costs chronically underbudgeted
findings.detail: The council is seeking £155k in additional costs for two supported housing facilities (Harper House and White House) to cover staffing, operational contracts, and void works that 'previous budgets did not allow for'. This includes £60k additional staffing and £88k for operational contract and void costs.
findings.matters: These are not one-off pressures but recurring costs the council has systematically underfunded; this suggests weak budget planning for council-run services.
findings.figures: £60k White House staffing + £59k White House operations + £29k Harper House operations + £7k Harper solar protection = £155k
findings.quote: Previous budgets did not allow for void works and/or the full cost of service contracts

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Unavoidable Expenditure Pressures 2026-27
findings.headline: Sustained HMO regulation backlog requiring £293k in agency and temporary staffing
findings.detail: The council is spending £100k on Environmental Health agency staff to reduce the HMO backlog, £133k on temporary Renters Rights officers, and £60k on Planning Enforcement to handle HMO work (starting March 2026). Total pressures: £293k across three service lines, all driven by one issue.
findings.matters: Systemic backlogs in HMO regulation suggest either demand surge or persistent capacity shortage; the reliance on temporary agency staffing indicates the council cannot recruit permanently for this work.
findings.figures: £100k agency (Environmental Health) + £133k temp staff (Renters Rights) + £60k Planning Enforcement = £293k
findings.quote: HMO agency for 2627 has been added to further reduce the backlog of HMO applications 100 ... 2X EH Renters Rights Technical Officers 133 ... £60k to cover increased work, which cannot be absorbed by the existing team planning enforcement team.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Unavoidable Expenditure Pressures 2026-27
findings.headline: Heathrow DCO examination costs will not be recovered from the applicant
findings.detail: The council is budgeting for senior officer resource (£60k) to manage the Development Consent Order process for Heathrow expansion. However, the document explicitly states that examination phase costs must be funded by the council and 'will not be subject to cost recovery', even though cost recovery from the applicant is still being negotiated.
findings.matters: A major infrastructure project is imposing unbudgeted costs on the council that it cannot recover; this represents an unquantified contingent liability.
findings.figures: £60k budgeted; examination costs unbudgeted and unquantified
findings.quote: Any costs incurred through the Examination of the DCO will need to be funded by the LPA's and will not be subject to cost recovery.

This is a formal governance intervention triggered by performance failures and means the council's decision-making is now subject to external oversight.
findings.matters: Central government intervention is a structural red flag for lending risk; it signals the council has failed statutory duties and cannot be trusted to self-correct.
findings.figures: £490k annual cost for commissioners
findings.quote: Finance & Corporate Services Commissioners 490 Appointed by the central government under Best Value duty directive (Local Government Act 1999)

findings.paper_title: SBC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 excl appendices
findings.headline: Council is being abolished in 14 months, creating transition risk and discontinuity
findings.detail: Spelthorne will cease to exist on 31 March 2027 due to local government reorganisation in Surrey. Any capital projects ongoing will transfer to the successor authority (West Surrey). Spending plans beyond 2026/27 are indicative only.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand there is no continuity of council decision-making or accountability after 31 March 2027. The successor authority may revise asset rationalisation plans or debt reduction strategy.

findings.paper_title: SBC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 excl appendices
findings.headline: Cash balances reducing significantly during 2026/27 to relatively low levels
findings.detail: The council held £37.2m in cash and short-term investments at December 2025, with £30m already committed to inter-authority lending. Balances are forecast to reduce to an average of £13.5m during 2026/27. This leaves limited liquidity buffer for operational contingencies.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's liquidity position as it enters a critical period of asset sales and debt reduction. Lower balances increase vulnerability to cash flow shocks.
findings.figures: £37.2m current balances; £13.5m forecast average in 2026/27; £30m already in inter-authority lending
findings.quote: The medium-term cashflow forecast is that balances will remain around this level for the remainder of 2025/26, but reduce to an average balance of £13.5m during 2026/27

findings.paper_title: SBC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 excl appendices
findings.headline: Subsidiary company has generated operating losses for six consecutive years
findings.detail: Knowle Green Estates Ltd, a council-owned company, has generated operating losses for the past six years. The council advanced £44.8m in soft loans to subsidiaries funded by borrowing, which do not generate financial return. The council commissioned an independent review of KGE's viability.
findings.matters: The council is funding loss-making operations via borrowing, adding to debt servicing burden. Viability of the company is uncertain, creating contingent liability risk.
findings.figures: £44.8m in loans to council companies; six consecutive years of operating losses at Knowle Green Estates
findings.quote: Both companies generated trading losses in 2024/25. In the case of Knowle Green Estates, the company has generated an operating loss for the past 6 years

findings.paper_title: SBC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 excl appendices
findings.headline: Capital financing costs consume an unsustainably high proportion of revenue budget
findings.detail: The ratio of capital financing costs (interest and MRP) to net revenue stream is 319% in 2026/27, far exceeding normal local authority levels. Even including investment property income, the ratio is 85% in 2026/27. Comparator authorities are typically at 18% or less.
findings.matters: This shows the council's revenue base cannot support the cost of its debt, even with property income. It indicates structural unaffordability and dependence on asset sales rather than income.
findings.figures: Capital financing costs 319% of net revenue stream (2026/27); 254% actual (2024/25); comparator authorities typically 18%; ratio declining only if asset sales complete as forecast
findings.quote: The ratio of capital financing charges to the net revenue stream at 31 March 2030 remains high at 169%. Many comparator authorities are currently reporting a ratio of 18% or less

findings.paper_title: SBC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 excl appendices
findings.headline: Investment property portfolio is severely impaired with negative equity position
findings.detail: The £552m property portfolio (at book value) is financed by £715m of borrowing, creating a loan-to-value ratio of 164%. The portfolio has fallen 43% in value since acquisition. If disposed of at current market values, the council faces £442m in realised losses.
findings.matters: The balance sheet is in negative equity on this portfolio. A lender needs to understand the risk of forced sales at distressed prices and the path to recovery.
findings.figures: £552m property value; £715m borrowing; 164% loan-to-value ratio; £442m at-risk losses; 43% fall in value since acquisition
findings.quote: have fallen in value by 43% since they were acquired originally... the Council is at risk of realising losses of £442m from disposing of the investment portfolio at current values

findings.paper_title: SBC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 excl appendices
findings.headline: Entire debt reduction plan depends on realising £293m from asset sales, with major downside risk if sales slip
findings.detail: The council forecasts £293m in capital receipts from selling investment property over 10 years to reduce borrowing. The MRP forecast assumes £22.5m in 2025/26. If receipts slip by just £10m, MRP in 2026/27 increases by £3.3m. The council has engaged external advisors but sales have not yet completed.
findings.matters: The entire debt reduction strategy has a single point of failure. A lender needs to understand this dependency and probability of slippage, especially in a rising interest rate environment affecting property values.
findings.figures: £293m target receipts; £22.5m assumed for 2025/26; £3.3m MRP increase for every £10m slippage
findings.quote: if £22.5m is not fully achieved either due to sales slipping into the next financial year, or not achieving target sales value, then MRP in 2026/27 would increase. For example, if there is slippage of £10m in capital receipts, this would increase MRP in 2026/27 by £3.3m

findings.paper_title: SBC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 excl appendices
findings.headline: Council is under formal Statutory Direction requiring debt reduction and asset rationalisation
findings.detail: The Secretary of State issued Statutory Directions on 8 May 2025 requiring an Improvement and Recovery Plan including a comprehensive debt reduction plan and asset rationalisation programme. The council has ceased capital projects and no new borrowing is planned. This is a formal intervention indicating prior financial distress.
findings.matters: Statutory Direction indicates formal oversight failure and structural financial problems. A lender needs to understand the council is operating under government constraint.
findings.figures: £715m debt remaining after restructuring (was £1,057m); second highest debt per head of population of all English local authorities at £10,347 vs £1,268 average
findings.quote: On 8 May 2025, the Secretary of State issued the Council with Statutory Directions requiring the Council to implement an Improvement and Recovery Plan which includes the following actions... a comprehensive and strict debt reduction plan, demonstrating how overall capital financing requirement and external borrowing will be reduced

findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer's Section 25 statement confirms budget estimates are robust but notes that reserves are essential for sustainability: 'Hence essential that through the unitary transformation process significant longer-term savings are achieved.' This signals that current trajectory is not sustainable without major structural change.
findings.matters: This is the formal s151 officer assessment that reserves alone cannot sustain the council's financial position. It indicates the savings programme is insufficient.
findings.figures: £14.2m projected reserves by end of MTFS period

Hence essential that through the unitary transformation process significant longer-term savings are achieved.

findings.paper_title: Draft Detailed Revenue Budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy 2026-27 to 2028-29

findings.matters: Council is using maximum borrowing room without referendum. Further council tax flexibility is limited. The low proportion of council tax revenue controlled locally limits options.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 fin excl appendices
findings.headline: The £343m debt restructuring discount is being amortised over 10 years, masking the full underlying cost of servicing the historical £1.1bn borrowing
findings.detail: While the restructuring reduced nominal borrowing by 30% and generated a £343m discount, the council still carries the underlying historical debt from the property acquisition programme. The discount (£34.3m per year benefit) masks what would otherwise be significantly higher MRP and interest costs. Once the discount runs out after 2034/35, costs will spike unless the asset portfolio is substantially sold off.
findings.matters: The restructuring provides a temporary reprieve. The £343m discount makes the next ten years look affordable in revenue terms. But this is an accounting treatment that defers the real cost of the failed property acquisition strategy. Once it runs out, if the council has not sold the property portfolio, its revenue position will deteriorate sharply. A lender should be very focused on whether asset sales will actually happen before the discount ends.
findings.figures: £343m discount; £34.261m annual benefit for 10 years; discount terminates 31 March 2035
findings.quote: This generated a discount of £343m, which is being amortised to the General Fund over 10 years as required by Regulation 30C of the Local Authorities Capital Finance and Accounting) (England) Regulations 2003, as amended.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 fin excl appendices
findings.headline: Council will be abolished on 31 March 2027 and merged into West Surrey unitary authority, creating uncertainty for forward projections
findings.detail: Spelthorne will cease to exist as a local authority in 14 months. It will merge into a new West Surrey unitary. The capital programme projections beyond March 2027 are explicitly flagged as 'only indicative and will depend on the successor authority'. This creates uncertainty about strategy continuity and creates transition risks.
findings.matters: Local government reorganisation creates transition risk and uncertainty. The council's ability to execute a multi-year asset disposal and debt reduction strategy is undermined by the fact that leadership, strategy and continuity will transfer to a new organisation. Lenders may be uncertain about whether asset disposal proceeds are guaranteed or whether a new administration might change priorities.
findings.figures: Council abolished 31 March 2027
findings.quote: Council is asked to: Consider and approve the proposed Capital Strategy and Capital Programme for 2026/27 - 2029 as set out in this report. Reason for Recommendation: The Council is required to set a revenue and capital budget. The Council is under Statutory Direction to implement a strict debt reduction policy and to rationalise its asset base. Council to approve the new Strategy as set out in this report, noting that any projections beyond 31 March 2027 are only indicative and will depend on the successor authority.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 fin excl appendices
findings.headline: Council debt was restructured in November 2025, reducing borrowing by over 30% and generating a £343m accounting discount
findings.detail: The council restructured its loan debt portfolio in November 2025. This reduced long-term borrowing on the balance sheet by over 30% and generated a £343m discount, which is being amortised to the General Fund over 10 years under Regulation 30C. This is an unusual and material accounting move.
findings.matters: A £343m gain from debt restructuring suggests the council was able to refinance at better terms, reducing its debt servicing burden. However, the size and complexity of the restructuring — and the fact it appears to be a response to prior borrowing decisions that have gone wrong — is a governance concern. The discount helps near-term finances but the underlying borrowing remains high.
findings.figures: Borrowing reduced by over 30%; £343m discount amortised over 10 years; discount being amortised at £34.261m per year
findings.quote: The Council restructured its existing loan debt portfolio in November 2025 reducing the value of long-term borrowing on the balance sheet by over 30%. This generated a discount of £343m, which is being amortised to the General Fund over 10 years as required by Regulation 30C of the Local Authorities Capital Finance and Accounting) (England) Regulations 2003, as amended.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 fin excl appendices
findings.headline: Capital programme and debt reduction strategy depend on generating £26.5m of capital receipts in 2025/26; a £10m shortfall would increase MRP costs by £3.3m
findings.detail: The council's plan to reduce borrowing relies on selling assets. If capital receipts slip by £10m — either through delayed sales or lower-than-expected sale prices — Minimum Revenue Provision (the statutory amount set aside to repay debt) would increase by £3.3m in 2026/27. This means the whole debt reduction strategy is exposed to asset sales execution risk.
findings.matters: This quantifies the council's execution risk. It is dependent on a specialist external property advisor (not yet appointed) to sell £26.5m of assets in a single year. If that fails, the council's ability to service existing debt becomes less certain and revenue budgets come under further pressure.
findings.figures: £26.5m capital receipts expected 2025/26; £10m shortfall would increase MRP by £3.3m in 2026/27
findings.quote: Failure to achieve expected recepirs will impact MRP in 2026/27. For example, if capital receipts generated were either late or less than anticipated by £10m, this would increase MRP in 2026/27 by £3.3m.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 fin excl appendices
findings.headline: 95% of the investment property portfolio is concentrated in office accommodation near Heathrow
findings.detail: The £583m investment property portfolio is almost entirely in a single sector (office) and a single geography (Heathrow area). This creates extreme concentration risk: a single sector downturn or property market shift affects the entire portfolio.
findings.matters: Concentration risk of this magnitude — 95% in one asset class in one location — means the council has no diversification. Office markets near airports have been under pressure since 2020. A lender seeing this level of concentration would question whether the council understood portfolio risk at the point of investment.
findings.figures: £583m of £731m total long-term assets (80% of balance sheet) in investment property; 95% of investment property in office accommodation
findings.quote: The Council's investment property portfolio is 95% concentrated in one sector, namely, office accommodation in the surrounding area of Heathrow airport.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 fin excl appendices
findings.headline: Council is under Statutory Direction from the Secretary of State to implement a strict debt reduction plan
findings.detail: In May 2025 the Secretary of State issued Statutory Directions requiring the council to implement a strict debt reduction plan, sustainable capital and treasury strategies, and an asset rationalisation programme. This signals formal government intervention in the council's financial management.
findings.matters: Statutory Direction is a red flag for lending. It signals that the council cannot be trusted to manage its finances without ministerial oversight and compulsion. The council's capital programme was suspended in October 2023 on affordability grounds — after government intervention was needed, not before.
findings.figures: Statutory Direction issued May 2025
findings.quote: Subsequently the Secretary of State issued the Council with Statutory Directions in May 2025 which, in particular, require the Council to implement: a plan to ensure the Authority's capital, investment and treasury management strategies are sustainable and affordable, including an asset rationalisation programme for assets and commercial investments. a comprehensive and strict debt reduction plan

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 fin excl appendices
findings.headline: Investment property portfolio has lost 43% of its value since 2016 acquisition, an average loss of £51m per year
findings.detail: The council borrowed £1.1 billion between 2016–2019 to acquire investment properties, primarily office accommodation around Heathrow. The portfolio has fallen in value by £456m since acquisition. This represents a sustained, material erosion of the asset base that was meant to generate returns to support council services and regeneration.
findings.matters: Lenders assessing this council's judgment on capital deployment and asset management are seeing a decision to borrow £1.1bn for property that has lost nearly half its value in less than a decade. This is evidence of severely deficient due diligence and investment discipline.
findings.figures: £1.1 billion borrowed 2016–2019; portfolio value fallen £456m (43%); average annual loss £51m (7.3% per annum)
findings.quote: the investment property portfolio has fallen in value by £456m (i.e. 43%) since acquisition in 2016/2019 as shown in Chart 1 below. This is an average of £51m (i.e. 7.3%) per annum.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Section 25 Report - Section 151 Officer Report

findings.detail: The council has lent approximately £45.3 million to its wholly-owned subsidiary Knowle Green Estates to finance 174 residential rental units. findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether a subsidiary's £45.3 million of debt supported by rental income is reliable, whether rental income can absorb economic shocks, and whether ongoing strategic review means asset sales may be forced, reducing the income stream.

findings.matters: Nightly paid accommodation costs are an open-ended liability that rises with homelessness and housing costs. This is a sector-wide pressure that councils struggle to control and a material financial lever on budget outturn.

The officer estimates only £21.7 million will remain by end of 2025/26 after applying reserves to balance the current year budget.
findings.matters: A lender extending credit to a council with £715 million of outstanding debt and reserves declining to less than £22 million needs to assess both total leverage and whether remaining reserves can cover operational shocks.

The Section 151 Officer explicitly states this 'in the short term it places greater pressure on the Revenue Budget', forcing trade-offs between debt reduction (mandated by government directions) and revenue spending.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the competing pressures: the council is under statutory directions to reduce debt, but doing so immediately constrains operational cash flow.

findings.headline: £22.3 million of reserves consumed in 2023/24 and 2024/25 to absorb costs that should not have been incurred

It then drew a further £6.5 million in 2024/25 to absorb the impact of MRP on assets reclassified as surplus. These are one-off legacy costs, but they consumed reserves that should have been retained for contingency.
findings.matters: A lender funding a council that has just burned £22.3 million on historical cost write-offs needs to know how much remains, what it is committed to, and whether reserves can absorb further shocks.

Both required management correction. These errors indicate the council's financial controls are not detecting material mistakes.

This formal Value for Money weakness is reported separately and indicates systemic governance issues in how the council manages spending and monitors effectiveness.
findings.matters: VFM weaknesses signal inadequate resource management and oversight, which directly affects financial stability and the council's ability to control costs.

findings.detail: The council's capital financing calculations do not reconcile with the balance sheet. A £17.6m gap exists that the council must investigate and correct. The CFR determines how much the council can borrow and is central to debt servicing capacity, so this unresolved discrepancy raises questions about the accuracy of borrowing calculations and available repayment headroom.
findings.matters: Capital Financing Requirement is fundamental to understanding a council's debt capacity and sustainability; an unexplained £17.6m gap indicates either miscalculated borrowing capacity or undisclosed capital commitments.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Annual Audit Report with changes highlighted
findings.headline: Auditors will disclaim their opinion on 2024/25 financial statements, unable to form a view on the council's financial position for the second consecutive year
findings.detail: The audit cannot be completed by the 28 February 2026 backstop date because there is no assured opening position from the prior year's disclaimed audit. This means the council's reported financial position and reserves cannot be independently verified. The council has now experienced five years of disclaimed audits from previous auditors, followed by a disclaimer expected in both 2023/24 and 2024/25.
findings.matters: Lenders depend on audited financial statements to assess borrowing risk; a disclaimed opinion means the council's financial position is unverified and cannot be relied upon.

findings.detail: The January 2026 audit report identified audit findings, showing a significant reduction from 2023-24. The S151 Officer notes the progress is positive but emphasises ongoing work is needed.

findings.quote: It is positive to note the progress made by the Finance team in reducing the number of audit findings, however, the Council need to continue to work with the auditors in rebuilding the assurance to move towards achieving non-disclaimed opinions in the future, in line with the Improvement and Recovery Plan objectives.

The report explicitly cites this unaffordable level as the reason for the Statutory Direction.
findings.matters: The council's revenue income cannot sustain its capital financing charges; this level of cost is structurally unsustainable and indicates financial distress
findings.figures: Affordability ratio 315% (estimate 262%), including property income 83% (estimate 71%), comparable authorities <18%
findings.quote: However, this remains well above the affordability ratio for comparable authorities which is less than 18%. This is one of the reasons for the Statutory Direction requiring the Authority to implement a treasury management strategy which is sustainable and affordable.

findings.paper_title: TM Outturn 2024-25 070725 v4.3 TC and PR comments 0807 and TC 1107
findings.headline: Secretary of State issued Statutory Direction on 8 May 2025 requiring Improvement and Recovery Plan with asset rationalisation and debt reduction
findings.detail: The council was placed under formal Statutory Direction requiring an Improvement and Recovery Plan including sustainable capital and treasury management, asset rationalisation of properties and commercial investments, and a comprehensive strict debt reduction plan. This is formal central government intervention in response to financial unsustainability.
findings.matters: Statutory Direction is extraordinary intervention signalling the council's financial strategy is fundamentally unsustainable and imposes mandatory restructuring; this materially increases credit risk
findings.figures: Direction issued 8 May 2025, after year-end 31 March 2025
findings.quote: Since the 31 March 2025, the Secretary of State issued the Council with Statutory Directions on 8 May 2025 requiring the Council to implement an Improvement and Recovery Plan

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement - Final
findings.headline: Knowle Green Estates (wholly-owned housing company) viability is uncertain; external experts commissioned to review long-term options; conflict of interest only recently remedied.
findings.detail: The council's subsidiary housing company, Knowle Green Estates Ltd (KGE), had governance issues including the S151 Officer serving on the Board (conflict of interest), a situation only remedied in January 2025. The AGS notes: 'as part of the Housing and Regeneration theme of the IRP, the Council has commissioned external experts to review KGE's long term viability and to suggest options.' KGE did acquire 81 temporary and permanent housing units using Local Authority Housing Fund capital, but the review suggests this is now being questioned.
findings.matters: Uncertainty about a material subsidiary's viability creates off-balance-sheet risk and indicates the council's housing and regeneration strategy may be unaffordable. The recent remediation of conflict-of-interest governance suggests prior decisions may not have been properly scrutinized.
findings.figures: KGE acquired 81 TA and resettlement properties using LAHF; independent review commissioned; conflict of interest remedied January 2025
findings.quote: as part of the Housing and Regeneration theme of the IRP, the Council has commissioned external experts to review KGE's long term viability and to suggest options.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement - Final
findings.headline: Financial governance failures spanned years (back to 2018-19) but went undetected due to five-year audit gap; external audit now finding material issues in accounts.
findings.detail: The Leader and Chief Executive state in the AGS: 'This feedback relates to issues which had developed over a period of years, going back to 2018-19, and would have been more promptly addressed if the Council had not gone through a five year period without the benefit of external audits.' Grant Thornton has issued a disclaimed opinion for 2023-24 because the council's opening balances could not be verified following the five-year audit gap. Grant Thornton issued seven key recommendations covering financial, governance, assets, procurement and risk management issues. The council and previous auditor BDO cleared statements for 2017-18 to 2022-23 using disclaimed opinions.
findings.matters: A five-year audit gap allowed material financial governance issues to accumulate undetected. The subsequent disclaimed opinion on 2023-24 accounts means the council's financial position cannot be independently verified, a critical risk for lending decisions.
findings.figures: Audit gap: 2017-18 to 2022-23; disclaimed opinions issued for this period; disclaimed opinion on 2023-24 due to inability to verify opening balances; Grant Thornton issued 7 key recommendations
findings.quote: This feedback relates to issues which had developed over a period of years, going back to 2018-19, and would have been more promptly addressed if the Council had not gone through a five year period without the benefit of external audits.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement - Final
findings.headline: Sinking fund reserves strategy is under review; council anticipates need to hold higher reserves to cushion future tenant churn and lease renewal risk.
findings.detail: The council maintains Sinking Funds Reserves of £34.3m to protect against short-term rental income volatility. However, a 'major refresh of our sinking fund modelling' during 2024-25 'identified the need over time to put more funds into the reserves to ensure that in future years that we have a sufficient safety cushion when leases for key tenants come up for renewal.' The AGS notes 'we will need to take a significantly more cautious view with respect to the amount of funds required to be set aside over time.' The rationale for holding these reserves is changing due to the planned asset rationalisation programme.
findings.matters: An increase in required sinking fund provisions reduces resources available for service delivery and indicates the council is recognizing higher operational risks in its property portfolio. The need for 'more cautious' reserves signals management's concern about tenant retention.
findings.figures: Sinking Funds Reserves: £34.3m at end 2024-25; major refresh of modelling undertaken; occupancy rate 90%
findings.quote: The Council during 2024-25 did a major refresh of our sinking fund modelling which in turn informed our medium term financial projections which identified the need over time to put more funds into the reserves to ensure that in future years that we have a sufficient safety cushion when leases for key tenants come up for renewal.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement - Final
findings.headline: Investment properties contribute 38% of council income, with occupancy at 90% at year-end and collection rate declining from 99.1% to 98.8%, indicating revenue concentration risk.
findings.detail: The council states explicitly: 'Thirty eight percent of the money we need to run the Council and provide services for residents now comes from our investment properties.' The commercial property portfolio achieved 98.8% collection of invoiced rents in 2024-25, down from 99.1% in 2023-24. Occupancy was 90% at year-end. The AGS notes 'there is a projected Budget gap...when it is expected that all the Surrey councils will see a drop in government funding', making the council unusually dependent on commercial income to cover statutory services.
findings.matters: A council deriving 38% of its income from commercial rents is unusually exposed to property market downturn, tenant defaults, and lease void periods. Declining collection rates and occupancy at 90% are early indicators of revenue stress.
findings.figures: 38% of income from investment properties; 98.8% collection rate (down from 99.1%); 90% occupancy at year-end; Sinking Funds Reserves at £34.3m
findings.quote: Thirty eight percent of the money we need to run the Council and provide services for residents now comes from our investment properties.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement - Final
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) policy was underfunded and has been urgently revised; underfunded MRP is a long-term financial liability.
findings.detail: The S151 Officer notes in their statement that 'the Council has a compliant Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) Policy (Minimum Revenue Provision being the requirement that Councils make provision to pay down unfinanced capital expenditure over a prudent period of time), which has now been addressed by the Council approving a new MRP policy on 17th November 2025.' The Best Value Inspection explicitly recommended urgent review of 'current MRP provision with its external auditors, Grant Thornton, as it is underfunded'.
findings.matters: Underfunded MRP is a material liability that accelerates future budget pressures. The council was not setting aside sufficient funds to repay historic capital expenditure, creating a deferred financing burden that will constrain future resources.
findings.figures: New MRP policy approved 17 November 2025
findings.quote: The Council should urgently review its current MRP provision with its external auditors, Grant Thornton, as it is underfunded.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement - Final
findings.headline: Government Directions require immediate reduction of external debt held by the council, a strategic constraint on borrowing capacity.
findings.detail: The Best Value Inspection report and Directions made under the Local Government Act 1999 (8 May 2025) explicitly require the Council to reduce the level of external debt it holds. This is identified as 'a key focus of the Improvement and Recovery Plan' and will be achieved through a 'medium-term assets rationalisation programme'. The council notes this is being done 'in the context of Local Government Reorganisation' to ensure a sustainable 2026-27 budget.
findings.matters: A government Direction to reduce external debt limits the council's ability to finance capital investment and restricts refinancing options. This is a binding constraint that will shape future borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: Government Direction issued 8 May 2025; assets rationalisation programme underway
findings.quote: The Council during 2024-25 received the Best Value Inspection report and Directions (Spelthorne Borough Council: Directions made under the Local Government Act 1999 (8 May 2025)) which include a requirement to reduce the level of external debt the Council holds.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement - Final
findings.headline: External government intervention via Commissioners appointed May 2025 to oversee comprehensive recovery, citing 13 key recommendations from Best Value Inspection covering governance, finance, commercial strategy and culture.
findings.detail: Following a Best Value Inspection concluded January 2025 and published March 2025, the Secretary of State appointed Commissioners in May 2025 to oversee the Council's implementation of recommendations. The BVI report identified 13 recommendations covering governance, finance, commercial strategy and organisational culture. The council is implementing an Improvement and Recovery Plan (IRP) approved by Council on 23 October 2025, structured around five themes: Finance, Commercial, Housing & Regeneration, Governance, and Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.matters: Government-appointed Commissioners and a formal intervention regime indicate the council is considered at material risk of failure. This is the highest governance risk signal available and directly affects the council's creditworthiness.
findings.figures: 13 recommendations from Best Value Inspection; Commissioners appointed May 2025; IRP approved 23 October 2025; quarterly reporting to MHCLG required
findings.quote: Commissioners were appointed in May 2025 to oversee the Council's recovery, with a focus on implementing a comprehensive Improvement and Recovery Plan (IRP).

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement - Final
findings.headline: Internal audit opinion downgraded to 'limited assurance' on governance, risk management and internal control, reflecting systemic weaknesses.
findings.detail: The Southern Internal Audit Partnership (SIAP) is anticipated to issue a 'limited assurance' opinion on the overall adequacy and effectiveness of the council's framework of governance, risk management and control for 2024-25. The transition to SIAP, delayed agreement of the audit plan, and officer capacity constraints are cited as reasons, but the council also notes this will be reassessed 'throughout the completion of the 2024-25 internal audit plan and through the continued assessment of other relevant sources of assurance'.
findings.matters: An internal audit opinion of limited assurance is a material governance red flag for lenders. It signals the council's control environment cannot be relied upon to prevent significant error or fraud.
findings.figures: Limited assurance opinion anticipated for 2024-25; final conclusion reported to Audit Committee September 2025
findings.quote: From the work carried out to date, it is anticipated that internal audits overall conclusion on the framework of governance, risk management and control will conclude in a 'limited assurance' opinion.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement - Final
findings.headline: Budget deficit of just over £2m for 2026-27, projected to grow further once revised Medium-Term Financial Plan is finalized, to be closed via transformation, asset disposals and debt rescheduling.
findings.detail: The council identified an initial £4m budget gap for 2026-27 when the 2025-26 budget was set in February 2025. The AGS now projects 'just over £2m' for 2026-27 but explicitly states this will 'have increased by the time the revised MTFS is firmed up in autumn 2025'. The gap is to be addressed through transformation, debt rescheduling and asset disposals — no alternative funding source identified.
findings.matters: An unresolved structural deficit in a council's MTFS is a core lending risk. Dependence on asset sales and refinancing to balance the budget indicates constrained financial headroom.
findings.figures: £4m gap identified February 2025; now 'just over £2m' for 2026-27; will increase further pending autumn 2025 MTFS refresh
findings.quote: A balanced budget was achieved for 2025–26, but an initial projected £4m gap for 2026–27, was identified when 2025-26 Budget was set in February 2025-26, this will have increased by the time the revised MFTP is firmed up in autumn 2025 and is planned to be addressed through transformation, debt rescheduling and asset disposals.

findings.paper_title: MRP Policy report v3.1
findings.headline: Mitigation strategy depends on asset sales that would simultaneously eliminate £45m annual rental income stream
findings.detail: The council's plan to avoid reserve depletion relies on rationalising its investment and regeneration assets to realise capital receipts. However, disposing of investment properties would remove the current gross rental income of approximately £45m annually. The report identifies that failure to complete asset sales at current valuations or on the planned timescales would delay reduction of MRP and leave the council vulnerable.
findings.matters: Creates a new financial risk: the mitigation strategy trades reduced MRP for loss of major recurring income; failure to execute asset sales leaves council with neither benefit
findings.figures: £45m gross rental income currently; asset sales could reduce MRP from £59m to £30m by 2029/30; disposal of BP site in 2035/36 would reduce MRP to £7m
findings.quote: Disposal of investment propert ies would also remove the current gross rental income stream of c£45m each financial year.

findings.paper_title: MRP Policy report v3.1
findings.headline: £45m in long-term debtors and £50m discrepancy in capital expenditure records remain unreconciled to balance sheet
findings.detail: The council's balance sheet contains £45m in long-term debtors where the purpose and financing of the loans are still under investigation by management. Separately, the council's records of unfinanced capital expenditure are £50m less than the CFR calculated directly from the balance sheet. The report notes this could mean MRP should be £2m higher and that the council may not be fully complying with Regulation 27 (the obligation to charge MRP on all unfinanced capital expenditure).
findings.matters: These reconciliation failures suggest the financial statements contain material errors; the council may still be understating its true MRP obligation
findings.figures: £45m long-term debtors under investigation; £50m discrepancy between recorded and balance-sheet-derived unfinanced capital expenditure; potential additional MRP of £2m
findings.quote: Work is still ongoing to reconcile the Council's CFR and MRP calculations back to the Balance Sheet at 31 March 2025... long-term debtors of £45m are reported in the Statement of Accounts. Enquiries are ongoing to confirm the purpose for which the loans were advanced and the financing of the loans... the Council records of unfinanced capital expenditure are £50m less than the CFR calculated from the balance sheet. Consequently, MRP could be around £2m higher.

findings.paper_title: MRP Policy report v3.1
findings.headline: Council's Capital Financing Requirement exceeds £1 billion, described as one of the highest in the country relative to service budgets and population
findings.detail: The council's unfinanced capital expenditure, measured by the CFR, has grown to over £1bn. The report notes this is exceptionally high relative to the council's size and service budgets, and that continuing with current low MRP levels would adversely affect the overall financial position in the context of risks within the investment assets portfolio.
findings.matters: High CFR relative to service budgets indicates either excessive capital investment or that capital costs have not been properly charged to revenue; signals structural imbalance
findings.figures: CFR exceeds £1bn
findings.quote: Currently the Council's CFR exceeds £1bn, making it one of the highest in the country relative to service budgets and population size. By continuing with the current low levels of MRP set aside, the Council would retain a high CFR, adversely affecting its overall financial position in the context of the risks ahead with the investment assets portfolio.

findings.paper_title: MRP Policy report v3.1
findings.headline: Without mitigating actions, increased MRP will exhaust all usable revenue reserves by 31 March 2027, triggering section 114 notice
findings.detail: The report explicitly states that the increased MRP charge, if not mitigated by other measures, will deplete the council's usable revenue reserves entirely within 18 months. This would force the s151 officer to issue a section 114 notice and require the council to seek Exceptional Financial Support from MHCLG.
findings.matters: Section 114 notice is formal acknowledgment of financial crisis requiring government intervention; signals the council cannot balance its budget
findings.figures: All usable reserves extinguished by 31 March 2027
findings.quote: Increasing MRP to a prudent level, as required by the Statutory Direction will, without any additional mitigating action, extinguish all the Council's usable revenue reserves before 31 March 2027. In this situation, the S.151 Officer would be obliged to is sue a s.114 Notice and the Council would need to seek Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from MHCLG.

findings.paper_title: MRP Policy report v3.1
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision must increase 4.6x from £13m to £59.9m under statutory direction due to governance failures
findings.detail: MHCLG statutory directions from May 2025 require the council to update its MRP policy after the Best Value Inspection and external audit identified that MRP was set too low in previous years. The council's previous calculation method did not follow statutory guidance: it used 50-year asset lives without professional valuer input (now revised to 15-25 years), omitted MRP on surplus assets and third-party loans, and incorrectly applied annuity method to investment property.
findings.matters: This 4.6x increase signals fundamental governance failures in financial management and creates acute financial distress requiring external intervention
findings.figures: Current budget £13m → proposed £59.9m for 2025/26; previous calculations based on 50-year asset lives now corrected to 15-25 years
findings.quote: Statutory Directions issued by the Ministry for Housing Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) in May 2025 which alongside other requirements directs the Council to implement 'a plan to ensure the Authority is complying with all relevant rules and guidelines relating to the financial management of the Authority, including updating the minimum revenue provision (MRP) policy'

findings.paper_title: Debt rescheduling report updated
findings.headline: Discount of £361m is volatile and dependent on gilt rates; could swing by £103m if rates move 1%
findings.detail: The £361m discount is calculated at mid-October gilt rates of 4.5-4.75%. Sensitivity modelling shows that a 1% rise in gilt rates increases the discount to £444m, but a 1% fall reduces it to £258m. Gilt rates are volatile and susceptible to Budget announcements and market sentiment. The council must execute the rescheduling promptly before rates move materially.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the financial benefit is not guaranteed and could materially deteriorate if rates fall.
findings.figures: Base discount £361m at mid-October rates; range £258m to £444m depending on ±1% gilt rate move; each 10bp rate reduction = £700k annual refinancing cost saving
findings.quote: if the discount rate reduced by 1%, then the discount would reduce by £103m to £258m over 10 years ie £26m per annum as opposed to the £36m each year quoted above.

findings.paper_title: Debt rescheduling report updated
findings.headline: Structural budget deficit of £6m still projected for 2026-27 even after rescheduling
findings.detail: Rescheduling generates £36m annual credit over 10 years, but MRP (Minimum Revenue Provision) is increasing by £42m annually, interest costs by £7m, and other budget pressures exist. After netting off the rescheduling benefit, the council still faces a £6m deficit in 2026-27 before considering broader revenue pressures, and a cumulative £100m deficit over 11 years without further mitigation.
findings.matters: The rescheduling is not solving the underlying budget problem; further action (service cuts, asset sales, reserves draw-down) will be needed.
findings.figures: £6m deficit 2026-27; £100m cumulative deficit over 11 years; MRP increase £42m; interest increase £7m
findings.quote: without other mitigation measures, after taking into account the MRP movement there would be a net Budget deficit of £6m by end of 2026-27.

findings.paper_title: Debt rescheduling report updated
findings.headline: Entire strategy depends on asset disposal programme achieving £650m+ in capital receipts over 10 years
findings.detail: The model assumes the council will sell investment properties and surplus assets to generate capital receipts. If valuations are achieved, 80% of remaining debt could be repaid from proceeds. Without these sales at expected prices and timescales, the council cannot service the debt or meet its repayment obligations, and risks late payment penalties to PWLB or forced short-term borrowing at variable rates.
findings.matters: The entire risk mitigation rests on execution of property sales; if they fail or slip, the council's debt position deteriorates rapidly.
findings.figures: Expected capital receipts sufficient to repay 80% of remaining borrowing if debt is rescheduled; with asset sales would reduce interest from £24.8m to £6m annually
findings.quote: If these valuations were achieved, the Council could potentially generate sufficient capital receipts over the next 10 years to repay 80% of its remaining borrowing if debt rescheduling takes place.

findings.paper_title: Debt rescheduling report updated
findings.headline: Rescheduling transforms phased £14-17m annual repayments into a single £545m bullet due in 2046
findings.detail: The current repayment strategy spreads principal repayment at £14-17m annually over 50 years. Rescheduling replaces this with a single lump sum of £545m due in 2046, creating significant liquidity risk unless the council's asset disposal programme generates sufficient capital receipts to pay down debt before that date.
findings.matters: A lender is exposed to whether the council can find £545m in 2046 or refinance it; this is a material change in repayment risk.
findings.figures: Current repayment profile £14-17m per annum; proposed single repayment £545m in 2046
findings.quote: The Council's original borrowing strategy was to repay loan principal annually at a rate of around £14-17m per annum for the next 50 years. Rescheduling debt as set out in sections 3 and 4 above would potentially replace a phased principal repayment profile with a single debt repayment of £545m in 2046.

findings.paper_title: Debt rescheduling report updated
findings.headline: Annual interest costs rise by £7m per annum (29%) under rescheduling proposal
findings.detail: The rescheduling trades a £361m discount for higher interest rates. Interest costs rise from £24.9m to £32m annually (£7m increase) because the rescheduled debt will be charged at 5.5% average versus the current fixed rate of 2.4%. This is a permanent structural increase in financing costs.
findings.matters: A lender evaluates the council's ability to service debt; a £7m annual cost increase reduces resilience.
findings.figures: Current interest £24.9m per annum; future £32m per annum; 5.5% average rate vs 2.4% current; £7m annual increase
findings.quote: interest payable for the Council would rise from current £24.9m per annum (original 2025-26 Budget) to £32m in 2026-27, an increase of £7m per annum, and that this partially offset by applying one tenth of the discount or £36m.

findings.paper_title: Debt rescheduling report updated
findings.headline: Second-highest debt per capita of any English council (£10,347) with net liabilities of £300m+
findings.detail: The council has debt of £1.06bn (£10,347 per head), the second highest in England. The balance sheet shows a net liabilities position over £300m because asset values have fallen 45% since acquisition. The council was debt-free until 2016/17 but borrowed over £1bn 2016-2022, mainly for property investment (89% of debt).
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial resilience through debt metrics and balance sheet position; both are severely weak here.
findings.figures: Debt £10,347 per capita (second highest English local authority); net liabilities £300m+; asset values down 45%
findings.quote: Spelthorne Borough Council was debt-free until 2016/17. Borrowing transactions totalling over £1bn took place between 2016 and 2022, mainly to provide funding for: Investment Property acquisitions (89% of the debt)... the value of Investment Property and regeneration assets, which have fallen by c.45% since their original acquisition.

findings.paper_title: Debt rescheduling report updated
findings.headline: Council operating under formal Statutory Direction from MHCLG requiring comprehensive debt reduction
findings.detail: In May 2025, MHCLG issued Statutory Directions requiring the Council to implement a comprehensive and strict debt reduction plan. Without this rescheduling, the council would need to issue a s.114 notice and seek Exceptional Financial Support from MHCLG. This is formal financial supervision.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council is under formal central government oversight and has limited alternatives.
findings.figures: Direction issued May 2025; potential for s.114 notice and EFS application
findings.quote: Statutory Directions issued by MHCLG in May 2025 require the Council to implement " a comprehensive and strict debt reduction plan".

news_drafts.headline: Council operating under government-appointed commissioners following 2024 Best Value failure
news_drafts.lead: Commissioner-led councils are at elevated risk. A lender must understand the causes of the Best Value failure and the credibility of the recovery plan.

news_drafts.headline: Internal audit identified control weaknesses in credit note approval, debt monitoring, payment plans, and write-off records
news_drafts.lead: Control weaknesses in income and debt management affect a council's financial resilience and audit assurance; a lender would want to understand that the council has identified the gaps and is remediating them systematically.

news_drafts.headline: £26.3m investment property sinking funds being repurposed to close general budget gaps rather than their original purpose
news_drafts.lead: The asset disposal programme removes the investment income stream that these reserves were designed to protect. The council is now using these funds for day-to-day shortfalls, signalling revenue sustainability problems independent of the investment portfolio.
